# Why not a list {background-color="#0C234B"}

## The same job, twice

```python
# a list
depths_ft = []
for d in depths_m:
    depths_ft.append(d * 3.28084)

# an array
depths_ft = depths_m * 3.28084
```

::: {.fragment}
Shorter, yes. That is the least of it.
:::

## It is also much faster

```{pyodide}
#| edit: false
#| autorun: false
#| min-lines: 12
import time
import numpy as np

big_list = list(range(1_000_000))
big_array = np.arange(1_000_000)

t0 = time.perf_counter()
_ = [x * 2.5 for x in big_list]
list_ms = (time.perf_counter() - t0) * 1000

t0 = time.perf_counter()
_ = big_array * 2.5
array_ms = (time.perf_counter() - t0) * 1000

print(f"list:  {list_ms:7.1f} ms")
print(f"numpy: {array_ms:7.1f} ms  ->  {list_ms / array_ms:.0f}x faster")
```

::: {.fragment}
The loop still happens. It happens in compiled C instead of in Python.
:::

## Why you should care in *this* course

::: {.incremental}
- A Week 11 model grid is 40 × 60 — small
- A basin model is 500 × 800 × 12 layers ≈ 5 million cells
- The solver touches every one of them, every iteration, every time step
:::

::: {.fragment .due-notice}
At 5 million cells a 50× difference is the difference between a coffee break and
going home. This is not a style preference.
:::

## What an array is

```{pyodide}
#| autorun: false
#| min-lines: 6
import numpy as np

depths = np.array([31.2, 45.8, 88.4, 12.0, 67.3])

print(depths.shape)   # how big, in each dimension
print(depths.dtype)   # ONE type for everything in it
print(depths.ndim)    # how many dimensions
```

::: {.fragment}
Fixed size, one dtype, a shape. A list has none of those — which is exactly why
it can't be fast.
:::

# Arithmetic {background-color="#0C234B"}

## Elementwise, by default

```{pyodide}
#| autorun: false
#| min-lines: 8
import numpy as np

land_surface = np.array([730.0, 742.5, 715.0, 760.2, 728.8])
depth_to_water = np.array([31.2, 45.8, 88.4, 12.0, 67.3])

head = land_surface - depth_to_water
print(head)
print(head.mean(), head.max() - head.min())
```

::: {.fragment}
Array-with-array works position by position. Array-with-scalar applies the
scalar everywhere — that is **broadcasting**, and it is why `depths * 3.28084`
does what you expect.
:::

## Your turn: hydraulic gradients

Five well pairs. Compute the gradient for all of them at once, then find the
steepest.

```{pyodide}
#| setup: true
#| exercise: ex_grad
import numpy as np
head_up = np.array([412.5, 409.1, 405.0, 418.2, 402.7])
head_down = np.array([408.2, 404.8, 401.9, 410.0, 399.9])
distance = np.array([850.0, 620.0, 740.0, 1150.0, 400.0])
```

```{pyodide}
#| exercise: ex_grad
gradients = ______
steepest = ______
print(f"gradients: {np.round(gradients, 5)}")
print(f"steepest:  {steepest:.5f}")
```

::: {.hint exercise="ex_grad"}
::: {.callout-note collapse="false"}
## Hint

No loop. Subtract one array from the other, divide by the third — numpy lines
them up for you. `.max()` finds the largest.
:::
:::

::: {.solution exercise="ex_grad"}
::: {.callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Solution

```python
gradients = (head_up - head_down) / distance
steepest = gradients.max()
```

The steepest is `0.007` — the last pair, which has the *smallest* head drop of
the five but is only 400 m apart. Gradient is a ratio; neither number tells you
anything on its own.
:::
:::

# Two dimensions {background-color="#AB0520"}

## A grid is a 2D array

```{pyodide}
#| autorun: false
#| min-lines: 9
import numpy as np

heads = np.array([
    [412.1, 411.4, 410.2, 408.9, 406.3, 403.1],
    [412.0, 411.2, 409.8, 408.1, 405.7, 402.9],
    [411.8, 410.9, 409.1, 406.2, 405.1, 402.6],
    [411.7, 410.8, 409.6, 408.0, 405.4, 402.7],
])
print(heads.shape)      # (rows, columns)
print(heads.mean())     # collapses everything
```

## `axis` is what gets *collapsed*

```{pyodide}
#| autorun: false
#| min-lines: 6
print("axis=0 collapses the rows -> one value per column")
print(np.round(heads.mean(axis=0), 2))

print("\naxis=1 collapses the columns -> one value per row")
print(np.round(heads.mean(axis=1), 2))
```

::: {.fragment}
Say it as "the axis that disappears." Every other phrasing I've tried leads
people to pick the wrong one about half the time.
:::

## Your turn: pick the axis

Compute the mean head **in each column** — six numbers, one per column — and the
head drop from the west edge to the east edge, averaged over all rows.

```{pyodide}
#| setup: true
#| exercise: ex_axis
import numpy as np
heads = np.array([
    [412.1, 411.4, 410.2, 408.9, 406.3, 403.1],
    [412.0, 411.2, 409.8, 408.1, 405.7, 402.9],
    [411.8, 410.9, 409.1, 406.2, 405.1, 402.6],
    [411.7, 410.8, 409.6, 408.0, 405.4, 402.7],
])
```

```{pyodide}
#| exercise: ex_axis
column_means = heads.mean(axis=______)
total_drop = ______
print(f"column means: {np.round(column_means, 2)}")
print(f"mean west-to-east drop: {total_drop:.2f} m")
```

::: {.hint exercise="ex_axis"}
::: {.callout-note collapse="false"}
## Hint 1

You want six numbers out of a 4 × 6 array, so the dimension of length 4 — the
rows — has to disappear.
:::
:::

::: {.hint exercise="ex_axis"}
::: {.callout-note collapse="false"}
## Hint 2

Once you have `column_means`, the drop is just its first element minus its last.
:::
:::

::: {.solution exercise="ex_axis"}
::: {.callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Solution

```python
column_means = heads.mean(axis=0)
total_drop = column_means[0] - column_means[-1]
```

`9.07` m over six cells. If the cells are 250 m wide that is a gradient of about
0.0073 — steep for a basin, which is a hint that this grid is a teaching
example rather than a real one.
:::
:::

## Indexing

```python
heads[2, 3]      # one cell:  row 2, column 3
heads[2]         # a whole row
heads[:, 3]      # a whole column
heads[:2, :2]    # the top-left 2x2 block
```

::: {.fragment}
Row first, then column — the same order MODFLOW uses for
`[layer, row, column]`. Getting used to it now saves you in Week 11.
:::

::: {.fragment}
Slices are half-open: `[:2]` gives you rows 0 and 1, not 0 through 2.
:::

## Boolean masks

```{pyodide}
#| autorun: false
#| min-lines: 6
mask = heads < 406.0

print(mask.sum(), "cells below 406 m")
print(heads[mask])

heads_capped = np.where(heads < 406.0, 406.0, heads)
print(np.round(heads_capped[2], 1))
```

::: {.fragment}
`np.where(condition, if_true, if_false)` is the vectorized `if`. This is how you
set a boundary condition across a grid without writing a nested loop.
:::

## Your turn: find the well

One cell in this grid is drawn down relative to its neighbours. Find how many
cells sit below 406 m, and the value of the single lowest head.

```{pyodide}
#| setup: true
#| exercise: ex_mask
import numpy as np
heads = np.array([
    [412.1, 411.4, 410.2, 408.9, 406.3, 403.1],
    [412.0, 411.2, 409.8, 408.1, 405.7, 402.9],
    [411.8, 410.9, 409.1, 406.2, 405.1, 402.6],
    [411.7, 410.8, 409.6, 408.0, 405.4, 402.7],
])
```

```{pyodide}
#| exercise: ex_mask
n_below = ______
lowest = ______
print(f"{n_below} cells below 406 m; lowest is {lowest} m")
```

::: {.hint exercise="ex_mask"}
::: {.callout-note collapse="false"}
## Hint 1

`heads < 406.0` gives an array of `True`/`False`. Summing it counts the `True`s,
because `True` is 1.
:::
:::

::: {.hint exercise="ex_mask"}
::: {.callout-note collapse="false"}
## Hint 2

`.min()` works on the whole array at once — you don't need the mask for that
part.
:::
:::

::: {.solution exercise="ex_mask"}
::: {.callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Solution

```python
n_below = (heads < 406.0).sum()
lowest = heads.min()
```

`8` cells, lowest `402.6`. Note that the lowest value is on the *downgradient
boundary*, not at the well — the drawdown at 406.2 in row 2 is only anomalous
compared to its neighbours. Finding a well by looking for the global minimum
would have found the wrong cell.
:::
:::
